A lock provides mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one CPU at a time can hold the lock. If the programmer associates a lock with each shared data item, and the code always holds the associated lock when using an item, then the item will be used by only one CPU at a time. In this situation, we say that the lock protects the data item. Although a lock is an easy-to-understand concurrency control mechanism, it can limit performance by serializing concurrent operations on the data it protects.

7.1 Races

The lost update at line 16 is an example of a race. A race is a situation in which a memory location is accessed concurrently, and at least one access is a write. A race is often a sign of a bug, either a lost update (if the accesses are writes) or a read of an incompletely-updated data structure. The outcome of a race depends on the machine code generated by the compiler, the timing of the two CPUs involved, and how their memory operations are ordered by the memory system, which can make race-induced errors difficult to reproduce and debug. For example, adding print statements while debugging push might change the timing of the execution enough to make the race disappear.

The usual way to avoid races is to use a lock. Locks ensure mutual exclusion, so that only one CPU at a time can execute the sensitive lines of push; this makes the scenario above impossible. The correctly locked version of the above code adds just a few lines (highlighted in yellow):

The sequence of instructions between acquire and release is often called a critical section. The lock is said to be protecting list.

You can think of a lock as serializing concurrent critical sections so that they run one at a time, and thus preserve invariants (assuming the critical sections are correct in isolation). You can also think of critical sections guarded by the same lock as being atomic with respect to each other, so that each sees only the complete set of changes from earlier critical sections, and never sees partially-completed updates.

Though useful for correctness, locks inherently limit performance. For example, if two processes call kfree concurrently, the locks will serialize the two critical sections, so that there is no benefit from running them on different CPUs. We say that multiple processes conflict if they want the same lock at the same time, or that the lock experiences contention. A major challenge in kernel design is avoidance of lock contention in pursuit of parallelism. Xv6 does little of that, but sophisticated kernels organize data structures and algorithms specifically to avoid lock contention. In the list example, a kernel may maintain a separate free list per CPU and only touch another CPU’s free list if the current CPU’s list is empty and it must steal memory from another CPU. Other use cases may require more complicated designs.

7.2 Code: Locks

Xv6 has two types of locks: spinlocks and sleep-locks. We’ll start with spinlocks. Xv6 represents a spinlock as a struct spinlock. The important field in the structure is locked, a word that is zero when the lock is available and non-zero when it is held. Were there no concurrency, xv6 could acquire a lock with code like

Unfortunately, this implementation does not guarantee mutual exclusion in the face of concurrency. Two CPUs could simultaneously reach line 25, see that lk->locked is zero, and then both grab the lock by executing line 26. At this point, two different CPUs hold the lock, which violates the mutual exclusion property. What we need is a way to make lines 25 and 26 execute as an atomic (indivisible) step.

Xv6’s acquire uses the above loop (Section 7.6 will explain __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE). Each iteration swaps one into lk->locked and checks the previous value; if the previous value is zero, then we’ve acquired the lock, and the swap will have set lk->locked to one. If the previous value is one, then some other CPU holds the lock, and the fact that we atomically swapped one into lk->locked didn’t change its value.

response.evidence_note: The supplied excerpts define mutual exclusion, races, critical sections, and the unsafe check-then-set lock. They support a medium MCQ asking students to apply these concepts to a concrete scenario.

questions.stem:
A small kernel module manages a shared linked list using a single lock variable lk. Two CPUs can run the following two routines concurrently. Routine A inserts a new node into the list and then updates a shared counter. Routine B removes a node from the list and then updates the same counter. Both routines use the lock operations shown below.

1. The lock is represented by a field lk->locked, which is 0 when the lock is available and non-zero when it is held.
2. An unsafe acquire routine checks whether lk->locked is zero, and if so sets lk->locked to one, using two separate ordinary instructions.
3. A correct acquire routine repeatedly swaps the value one into lk->locked and checks the previous value; if the previous value was zero, the lock has been acquired.
4. Each routine places its list insertion or removal, and its counter update, between the acquire and release calls.
5. If two CPUs execute the unsafe acquire routine at the same time, both may see lk->locked as zero and both may set it to one.

Which statement best explains why using the unsafe acquire routine does not provide mutual exclusion for this scenario?

Claim 1: The unsafe acquire routine's check and set are not atomic, so both CPUs can pass the check before either sets lk->locked, allowing two critical sections to run concurrently.

Claim 2: The unsafe acquire routine fails only because the counter update is a read-modify-write, whereas the list operations are safe.

Claim 3: The unsafe acquire routine fails only because the list has two operations instead of one, so a single lock cannot protect both.

Claim 4: The unsafe acquire routine would be correct if Routine A and Routine B used the same lock, regardless of the check-and-set timing.
options: Claim 1 is correct; the check and set are separate steps in the unsafe routine, so two CPUs can both see lk->locked as zero and both enter their critical sections, while the atomic swap in the correct routine prevents this.
Claim 2 is correct; the counter update alone is the race, and the unsafe acquire routine would protect the list operations if they were moved outside the critical section.
Claim 3 is correct; a single lock cannot protect a list with two operations, so two locks are required regardless of whether acquire is atomic.
Claim 4 is correct; sharing the same lock between Routine A and Routine B is sufficient for mutual exclusion even if the check-then-set sequence is not atomic.
questions.explanation: A race occurs when a memory location is accessed concurrently and at least one access is a write. The unsafe acquire routine reads lk->locked and then writes it as two separate steps. Under concurrency, two CPUs can both read zero before either writes one, so both acquire the lock and run their critical sections at the same time; mutual exclusion is violated even though both routines share the same lock. The correct routine avoids this by making the swap-and-check an atomic step, so only one CPU can observe the previous value as zero.

Under concurrency, two CPUs can both read zero before either writes one, so both acquire the lock and run their critical sections at the same time; mutual exclusion is violated even though both routines share the same lock. The correct routine avoids this by making the swap-and-check an atomic step, so only one CPU can observe the previous value as zero.

questions.stem:
Two CPUs, C1 and C2, both run a routine that updates a shared counter counter. The intended update is a read-modify-write: each CPU reads counter into a local register, adds 1, and writes the result back. To prevent races, the programmer has associated one lock lk with counter. The only locking code available on this system is a 'check-then-set' acquire:

- Step 1: if lk->locked is zero, proceed to Step 2.
- Step 2: set lk->locked to one.

Assume shared memory is coherent, so both CPUs always see the same current value of lk->locked, but the two steps above are not executed as one indivisible operation.

Scenario:
C1 and C2 reach the acquire code at nearly the same time. C1 executes Step 1 and observes lk->locked is zero. C2 then executes Step 1 and also observes lk->locked is zero. C1 then executes Step 2, setting lk->locked to one. C2 then executes Step 2, setting lk->locked to one. Both CPUs then execute the counter update as a critical section and later release lk.

Statement 1: The sequence of instructions between acquire and release is called a critical section.
Statement 2: A lock provides mutual exclusion if only one CPU at a time can hold the lock.
Statement 3: The check-then-set code above guarantees mutual exclusion because each CPU checks lk->locked before setting it.
Statement 4: In this scenario, C1 and C2 could both hold lk at the same time, so the counter update is not protected as intended.

Based only on the supplied material and the scenario, which option best evaluates Statements 1-4?
options: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect because two CPUs can both observe lk->locked as zero, both proceed to set it to one, and thus both hold the lock, violating mutual exclusion.
Statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect because a lock guarantees mutual exclusion only if the check-and-set is performed by the same instruction on all CPUs.
Statements 2, 3, and 4 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect because a critical section is defined as any code that runs concurrently, whether or not a lock is associated with it.

Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct; Statement 4 is incorrect because once both CPUs have set lk->locked to one, the hardware prevents either from entering the critical section until the other releases.

sources.text:
A lock provides mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one CPU at a time can hold the lock. If the programmer associates a lock with each shared data item, and the code always holds the associated lock when using an item, then the item will be used by only one CPU at a time. In this situation, we say that the lock protects the data item. Although a lock is an easy-to-understand concurrency control mechanism, it can limit performance by serializing concurrent operations on the data it protects.

7.1 Races

The lost update at line 16 is an example of a race. A race is a situation in which a memory location is accessed concurrently, and at least one access is a write. A race is often a sign of a bug, either a lost update (if the accesses are writes) or a read of an incompletely-updated data structure. The outcome of a race depends on the machine code generated by the compiler, the timing of the two CPUs involved, and how their memory operations are ordered by the memory system, which can make race-induced errors difficult to reproduce and debug. For example, adding print statements while debugging push might change the timing of the execution enough to make the race disappear.

The usual way to avoid races is to use a lock. Locks ensure mutual exclusion, so that only one CPU at a time can execute the sensitive lines of push; this makes the scenario above impossible. The correctly locked version of the above code adds just a few lines (highlighted in yellow):

The sequence of instructions between acquire and release is often called a critical section. The lock is said to be protecting list.

You can think of a lock as serializing concurrent critical sections so that they run one at a time, and thus preserve invariants (assuming the critical sections are correct in isolation). You can also think of critical sections guarded by the same lock as being atomic with respect to each other, so that each sees only the complete set of changes from earlier critical sections, and never sees partially-completed updates.

Though useful for correctness, locks inherently limit performance. For example, if two processes call kfree concurrently, the locks will serialize the two critical sections, so that there is no benefit from running them on different CPUs. We say that multiple processes conflict if they want the same lock at the same time, or that the lock experiences contention. A major challenge in kernel design is avoidance of lock contention in pursuit of parallelism. Xv6 does little of that, but sophisticated kernels organize data structures and algorithms specifically to avoid lock contention. In the list example, a kernel may maintain a separate free list per CPU and only touch another CPU’s free list if the current CPU’s list is empty and it must steal memory from another CPU. Other use cases may require more complicated designs.

7.2 Code: Locks

Xv6 has two types of locks: spinlocks and sleep-locks. We’ll start with spinlocks. Xv6 represents a spinlock as a struct spinlock. The important field in the structure is locked, a word that is zero when the lock is available and non-zero when it is held. Were there no concurrency, xv6 could acquire a lock with code like

Unfortunately, this implementation does not guarantee mutual exclusion in the face of concurrency. Two CPUs could simultaneously reach line 25, see that lk->locked is zero, and then both grab the lock by executing line 26. At this point, two different CPUs hold the lock, which violates the mutual exclusion property. What we need is a way to make lines 25 and 26 execute as an atomic (indivisible) step.

Xv6’s acquire uses the above loop (Section 7.6 will explain __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE). Each iteration swaps one into lk->locked and checks the previous value; if the previous value is zero, then we’ve acquired the lock, and the swap will have set lk->locked to one. If the previous value is one, then some other CPU holds the lock, and the fact that we atomically swapped one into lk->locked didn’t change its value.
